Krzysztof Krainski
kzhish'tof kri-een'ske
n. (Krzysztof Krainski, 1556–1618, Polish Reformed superintendent, author of the Postylla and the Agenda)
Polish Krzysztof from Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; Krainski, of Kraina, a place-name surname.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Krzysztof Krainski was superintendent of the Reformed churches of Lesser Poland in the generation when the Counter-Reformation was closing in, and his two great books were written for churches that were losing ground. The Postylla supplied Polish expositions for the whole church year; the Agenda supplied the forms — how to baptise, how to administer the Supper, how to marry, how to bury, how to visit the sick and comfort the dying — so that a minister in an isolated congregation, or in the end a layman where no minister could come, had the order of the church in his hands. He also wrote a history of the Polish Reformed church. The dictionary names the Agenda as the more important of the two. A church under pressure loses its ministers first and its buildings second; what it can keep is a known form of sound words, and Krainski was writing to make sure that when the pastor was gone the people would still know how the church of Christ does things.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines agenda as a memorandum book of things to be done, and form as a model, a prescribed order of words.

expand to see more

AGEN'DA, n. A memorandum-book; among divines, the things to be done, as distinguished from matters of belief.

FORM, n. A model; a draught; a pattern; a prescribed order of words, as a form of prayer.

POS'TIL, n. A short comment or explanatory note on a text of Scripture.

AGEN'DUM, n. A thing to be done; a service to be performed.

Key Scripture

2Ti 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

1Co 11:2 — "Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you."

1Co 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Jer 6:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein."

Modern Corruption

His Agenda put the church's forms into the people's hands against the day the minister was taken away.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a contempt for forms as such, as though a settled order of words were the enemy of sincerity. Krainski was writing for congregations that would shortly have no minister, and his forms were the means by which an orphaned church could still baptise its children and bury its dead as Christians rather than inventing something.

The principle to recover is that sound words are given a pattern and the pattern is to be held. “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13). Paul commends a church for keeping delivered order: “keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you” (1Co 11:2). And the old path is to be asked for and walked in rather than improvised — “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern, an outline, a form; Greek paradosis (G3862), that which is delivered.

Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a pattern, a form; 2 Timothy 1:13.

Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, to be in health; 2 Timothy 1:13.

Greek paradosis (G3862) — an ordinance, that which is handed down; 1 Corinthians 11:2.

Hebrew nethibah (H5410) — a path, a way; Jeremiah 6:16.

Greek taxis (G5010) — order, arrangement; 1 Corinthians 14:40.

Usage

"“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — the Agenda written for churches about to lose their pastors."

"“keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you” (1Co 11:2) — baptism, Supper, marriage and burial set down."

"“ask for the old paths, where is the good way” (Jer 6:16) — a Postylla for the whole church year."
